description: We are a team of students from the National University of Chimborazo. Our interests include programming, software development, artificial intelligence, data analysis, and problem-solving. We want to explore how NASA data can be used to understand weather conditions, improve decisions about crop rotation, and help farmers adapt to climate change. We are looking for motivated team members with skills in agriculture, environmental science, programming, data science, and artificial intelligence.
summary: AgroCycle is a web app that helps agricultural technicians and farmers in Chimborazo, Ecuador, decide what to plant after each harvest. The technician outlines the plot on a satellite map, and the app retrieves NASA POWER (rainfall and temperature), SRTM (altitude and slope), the MODIS NDVI layer and SoilGrids (soil) data. It corrects temperature to the plot’s real altitude, since in the Andes a hundred meters changes frost risk. An agronomic simulator computes water, frost and soil health month by month for each crop. It compares three rotations against current practice and delivers a 12-month plan in plain language, flagging risky months, via WhatsApp or PDF. This addresses the challenge of comparing rotation strategies using NASA data. It matters because repeating the same crop depletes soil and builds up pests, and technicians need data to support their advice. The app is available in Spanish and English.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AgroCycle is a decision-support web app for planning crop rotation in the highlands of Chimborazo, Ecuador. The agricultural extension technician uses it together with the farmer, in five steps:

Register the plot: the technician taps the corners of the field on a satellite map and the app calculates the area in hectares and in cuadras, the local land unit. It also records the crop history, irrigation type and observed problems.

Retrieve NASA data by coordinates:

NASA POWER: monthly mean, minimum and maximum temperature and rainfall.

NASA SRTM 30 m: altitude and slope.

MODIS NDVI (NASA GIBS): vegetation cover.

SoilGrids (ISRIC): soil pH, organic matter and texture.

GPM IMERG and SMAP: used as a regional reference for heavy rainfall and soil moisture.

Adjust the data to the plot: a NASA POWER cell is about 50 km wide, so temperature is corrected to the plot’s real altitude (−0.58 °C per 100 m) and rainfall is checked against the local canton reference.

Simulate and compare: an agronomic model computes, month by month, the soil water balance, frost risk and expected yield of each crop. It tests every valid crop combination for the year and scores each one from 0 to 100 on soil, water, climate, plant health and income. It then compares the top 3 against what the farmer plants today.

Deliver the plan: a 12-month plan in plain language that flags the months with frost, drought or bare-soil risk, sent by WhatsApp or PDF. A “What if…?” simulator tests dry, wet, warmer or frostier years.

Benefits

Recommendations backed by satellite data, not only by habit.

Fewer pests and diseases by switching crop families.

Fertilizer savings, because legumes such as faba bean and Andean lupin leave nitrogen in the soil.

Less erosion, by keeping the soil covered in critical months.

Farmers know in advance which months carry frost or drought risk.

Technicians can serve more families with clear, verifiable information.

Expected impact

Improve soil health and harvest stability for Andean smallholders, who often plant the same crop over and over. In the short term we plan a pilot with farmer associations in Chimborazo. Then we aim to extend the tool to other highland provinces and offer it to farmer associations, local governments and NGOs. Farmers use it for free through their technician.

Tools used

Language: Python.

Web interface: Streamlit.

Maps: Folium and Leaflet, with satellite imagery.

Charts: Plotly.

Data: pandas, SQLAlchemy and SQLite.

APIs: requests, for NASA POWER, SRTM, NASA GIBS and SoilGrids.

PDF: fpdf2.

Quality: automated tests with pytest.

Code and deployment: GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud.

No special hardware: it runs in the browser on a computer or a phone.

How is it creative?

It turns global NASA data into a concrete local decision: what to plant, in which order and when, on a field smaller than one hectare.

It corrects climate data for altitude, which is key in the Andes, where a few hundred meters change the frost risk.

It is not a “black box”: each option explains why it is recommended, which data support it, which data are missing and what the technician should check in the field.

It speaks the farmer’s language: a simple view for farmers and a technical view, plans delivered by WhatsApp, and a full Spanish/English interface.

What did the team take into account?

The real user: extension technicians and farmers with little digital experience. That is why the app has an easy map, a quick guide and jargon-free language.

The Andean reality: local crops (potato, faba bean, quinoa, Andean lupin, oats, barley), frost, steep slopes and erosion.

Honesty about the data: we use the typical climate of each month rather than made-up forecasts, and we test difficult years with scenarios. Scores are for comparing options, not for measuring fertility, and GPM and SMAP are clearly labeled as regional references.

Reliability: if a data source does not respond, the app falls back to stored real data and says so. Data are cached so the app does not always depend on the internet.

The technician’s judgment: the technician reviews and validates every plan before it is delivered; the tool does not replace them.
